Chapter 3. The Rise of Fundamentalist Sects.
As the mainstream Mormon church started moving away from its most controversial practices, a new kind of believer quietly emerged. These were men and women who felt deeply betrayed by the changes—convinced the church had turned away from its true purpose. For them, giving up polygamy wasn’t just a new policy. It was a sign the church had lost its way.
In hidden valleys and small, out-of-the-way towns, little groups began to gather—determined to keep the old traditions alive. They called themselves fundamentalists, holding tight to those teachings that once defined their faith. For these folks, the words of the early prophets didn’t belong to history books. They were living commandments, meant to be followed, no matter the cost.
Life in these communities was shaped by a real sense of separation. The outside world? It was seen as corrupt, even dangerous—a place where true believers just couldn’t survive. Inside the group, loyalty meant everything. Leaders claimed they spoke for God, demanding obedience and sacrifice from everyone who followed them. The rules were strict, and the punishments? Often severe.
You know, for a lot of people, the draw of fundamentalism was all about certainty. In a world full of questions and compromise, these communities offered clear answers and a powerful sense of purpose. The line between right and wrong was drawn in bold, and anyone who started to question the rules risked being cast out.
But belonging came at a steep price. Women and children especially felt the weight of what the community expected. Plural marriage wasn’t just allowed—it was required, almost a badge of spiritual strength. Dissent was risky, and those who tried to leave often found themselves cut off from everything—and everyone—they’d ever known.
The story of fundamentalist Mormonism is complicated. It’s filled with hope and heartbreak. For some, it was a chance to live out their deepest convictions, to build a life that felt meaningful and true. For others, it became a prison—a place where fear and control replaced love and trust.
The Lafferty brothers, whose actions would one day shock the nation, found themselves pulled into this world. Disillusioned with the mainstream church, they went searching for fundamentalist teachings, convinced they’d been chosen for something special. Their journey became more and more isolated as they cut ties with friends and family who didn’t share their beliefs.
In this insular world of fundamentalism, the brothers found validation for even their most extreme ideas. Surrounded by others who shared their longing for purity, they started seeing themselves as instruments of God’s will. And that thin line between faith and fanaticism? It started to disappear.
Most people never come face-to-face with this kind of extremism. From the outside, it’s hard to imagine how ordinary men and women could embrace beliefs so radical. But on the inside, the logic feels almost undeniable. When every moment is shaped by the belief that God is always watching, even the most unthinkable actions can start to seem not just justified—but necessary.
